## Last Time{.smaller}

A teacher wants to know whether using a new study app causes students to be more likely to pass an exam.

The teacher has 100 students who agree to participate. She randomly assigns:

| Group        | Passed | Total |
| ------------ | -----: | ----: |
| Study App    |     42 |    50 |
| No Study App |     34 |    50 |

$Ho: p_1 - p_2 = 0$

$Ha: p_1 - p_2 > 0$

$\hat{p_1} = \frac{42}{50} = 0.84$

$\hat{p_2} = \frac{34}{50} = 0.68$

## Wait 

We notice $\hat{p_1} = \frac{42}{50} = 0.84$ and $\hat{p_2} = \frac{34}{50} = 0.68$...

Those numbers are different...

... why can't we just say we have evidence to suggest the study app works? 

# Variability 

## Variability 

Statistics all comes down to quantifying variability/uncertainity...

We are in the hypothesis testing game of trying to figure out "did we see something unusual enough" to the point where we have evidence to reject our initial claim. **We would never expect our sample statistic to be exactly our parameter value** in the first place. The question isn't are they equal, the question is is our result unusual. 

## Assumptions 

"can trust the results of our test..."

Carful phrasing to help us remember that if our assumptions our violated... we can't trust our results. 

... it doesn't stop us from calculating anything!



## Central Limit Theorem 

Independence of observations

For quantitative data:

-- n > 30

For categorical data:

-- Success/Failure Condition (> 10)

## Checking assumptions 

Success/Failure 

-- How many successes would you expect to see under the assumption of your null hypothesis?

-- How many failures would you expect to see under the assumption of your null hypothesis?

## Checking assumptions 

$H_o$: $p_1 = p_2$

Without the jargon, this means that the groups don't matter! It doesn't matter if you were assigned to use the study app or not. 

If the groups don't matter, how many successes did we observe? How many failures? 

## Checking assumptions 

$p_{pooled}$ = $\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\text{success}_1 + \text{success}_2}{n_1 + n_2}$


$$
\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}}
=
\frac{\text{success}_1+\text{success}_2}{n_1+n_2}
=
\frac{42+34}{50+50}
=
0.76
$$

## Checking assumptions 

$$
n_1\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}} = 50(0.76) = 38
$$
$$
n_1(1-\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}}) = 50(0.24) = 12 
$$
$$
n_2\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}} = 50(0.76) = 38 
$$

$$
n_2(1-\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}}) = 50(0.24) = 12
$$

$$
38,\ 12,\ 38,\ 12 \geq 10
$$


## Sampling Distribution 

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# Null hypothesis: p1 = p2
p_pooled <- 0.76
n1 <- 50
n2 <- 50

# Standard error under H0
SE <- sqrt(p_pooled * (1 - p_pooled) * (1/n1 + 1/n2))

# Create values for the sampling distribution
x <- seq(-0.5, 0.5, length.out = 1000)

# Normal density under H0
data <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  density = dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = SE)
)

ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Null Sampling Distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂",
    subtitle = "Assuming the null hypothesis is true",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

What's the spread of the distribution? 

## Standard Error{.smaller} 

$$
SE_{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2}
=
\sqrt{
\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}}
(1-\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}})
\left(
\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}
\right)
}
$$

$$
SE_{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2}
=
\sqrt{
(0.76)(0.24)
\left(
\frac{1}{50}+\frac{1}{50}
\right)
}
$$

$$
SE_{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2}
=
\sqrt{0.007296}
\approx 0.0854
$$

## Hypothesis Test 

And we could conduct the hypothesis test here! 

BUT 

We tend to standardize so we can to: 

-- Compare against other studies 

-- Nice z-statistic interpretation 

So let's do it! 

## z-statistic 

How do we standardize our statistic? 

## z-statistic 

$$
z =
\frac{\text{observed statistic} - \text{null value}}
{\text{standard error}}
$$
... and we know these things!

## z-statistic 

$$
z =
\frac{
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 - (p_{1o} - p_{2o})
}{
\sqrt{
\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}}
(1-\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}})
\left(
\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}
\right)
}
}
$$

## z-statistic 

$$
z =
\frac{
(0.84-0.68)-0
}{
\sqrt{
(0.76)(0.24)
\left(
\frac{1}{50}+\frac{1}{50}
\right)
}
}
= \approx 1.87
$$

## Hypothesis Test

For this, assume that $\alpha = 0.05$


Draw how the p-value is calculated

## Hypothesis Test

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)

# Create standard normal distribution
data <- data.frame(
  z = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
)

data$y <- dnorm(data$z)

# Data for the shaded p-value region
shade <- subset(data, z >= 1.87)

ggplot(data, aes(x = z, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "black") +
  
  # Shade the p-value
  geom_area(
    data = shade,
    aes(x = z, y = y),
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Mark z = 1.87
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1.87,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Label
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2.35,
    y = 0.08,
    label = "p-value",
    color = "steelblue",
    size = 5
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.87,
    y = 0.42,
    label = "z = 1.87",
    color = "red",
    size = 5
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Standard Normal Distribution",
    subtitle = "Right-tailed test",
    x = "z",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```

## p-value 

Before clicking that button, guess what the p-value is going to be!

```{webr-r}
pnorm(1.87, 0, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

# Questions 

## Hypothesis Testing 

Our hypothesis test helped us gain evidence (or lack of) for some alternative range of values....

... but this doesn't really help us **estimate** plausible values of our population parameter.

How could we do that?

## Confidence Interval 

We want to estimate plausible values of $p_1 - p2$! 

Let's talk about the intuition behind this. 

## Context 

A teacher wants to know whether using a new study app causes students to be more likely to pass an exam.

The teacher has 100 students who agree to participate. She randomly assigns:

| Group        | Passed | Total |
| ------------ | -----: | ----: |
| Study App    |     42 |    50 |
| No Study App |     34 |    50 |

Based on the data, what is your best guess of $p_1 - p2$?

How do you feel about this guess? Is it right?

## Context

You can make an educated guess using your sample data... but you probably don't think that is equal to $p_1 - p_2$. 

So, let's take our best guess and quantify some variability around it!

$\hat{p_1} = \frac{42}{50} = 0.84$

$\hat{p_2} = \frac{34}{50} = 0.68$

$\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2} = .16$

## Goal 

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)

# Sample proportions
p1 <- 42/50
p2 <- 34/50

# Difference in sample proportions
diff <- p1 - p2

# Standard error for the sampling distribution
SE <- sqrt((p1 * (1 - p1) / 50) +
           (p2 * (1 - p2) / 50))

# Create x-values
x <- seq(diff - 4*SE, diff + 4*SE, length.out = 1000)

# Normal density
df <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  y = dnorm(x, mean = diff, sd = SE)
)

# Plot
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = diff, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distribution of Difference in Sample Proportions",
    x = "Difference in Sample Proportions",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The standard error is ~ 0.0839

## Goal

Our goal is to make a 95% confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$

```{r}
#| echo: false
lower <- diff - 1.96 * SE
upper <- diff + 1.96 * SE

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = diff, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lower, upper),
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distribution with 95% Confidence Interval",
    x = "Difference in Sample Proportions",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Difference 

This is the sampling distribution from hypothesis testing... how are they different?


```{r}
#| echo: false

library(ggplot2)

# Null hypothesis: p1 = p2
p_pooled <- 0.76
n1 <- 50
n2 <- 50

# Standard error under H0
SE <- sqrt(p_pooled * (1 - p_pooled) * (1/n1 + 1/n2))

# Create values for the sampling distribution
x <- seq(-0.5, 0.5, length.out = 1000)

# Normal density under H0
data <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  density = dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = SE)
)

ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Null Sampling Distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂",
    subtitle = "Assuming the null hypothesis is true",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


The standard error is ~ 0.0854

# Questions 

## Checking Assumptions 

Independence of observations

For quantitative data:

-- n > 30

For categorical data:

-- Success/Failure Condition (> 10)

but with a slight twist for confidence intervals...

## Before 

$p_{pooled}$ = $\hat{p}_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\text{success}_1 + \text{success}_2}{n_1 + n_2}$

why did we do this?

## Now 

We don't have a null hypothesis to assume true... 

We use the observed proportions to check the success failure condition!

Check your success failure condition now!

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Study App:} \quad
&50(0.84)=42>10 \\
&50(1-0.84)=8<10 \\[6pt]
\text{No Study App:} \quad
&50(0.68)=34>10 \\
&50(1-0.68)=16>10
\end{aligned}
$$

## Assumptions

... in practice... this would give us pause

We will continue moving forward under the idea that there is not enough evidence to violate our assumptions


## Confidence interval 

So now, we need to calculate this interval. What's the formula?

```{r}
#| echo: false
lower <- diff - 1.96 * SE
upper <- diff + 1.96 * SE

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = diff, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lower, upper),
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distribution with 95% Confidence Interval",
    subtitle = "SE ~ 0.0839",
    x = "Difference in Sample Proportions",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Formula 

$\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2} \pm z^* * SE(\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2})$

What is $z^*$?

## z*

$z^*$ is the critical value that tells you how many standard errors you need to go out from your sample statistic to capture the desired confidence level.

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(
  x = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
)

df$y <- dnorm(df$x)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-2.0, 2.0),
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.0, y = 0.05,
           label = "t*", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.0, y = 0.05,
           label = "-t*", color = "red") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "95% Confidence Interval",
    x = "Standard Deviations from 0",
    y = "Density"
  )
```


## z*

We can use $z^*$ because the sampling distribution of our statistic $\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2}$ is normal. 

On a normal distribution with mean 0 and SD of 1.... 1.96 standard deviations away from the CONTAINS 95% of the distribution! 

Our statistic $\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2}$ is normally distributed, it just has a different measure of spread. 

## Formula 

$\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2} \pm z^* * SE(\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2})$

1.96 standard errors away from the center will contain 95% of our sampling distribution! 

## z*

How do we know 1.96?

```{webr-r}
qnorm(.975, 0, 1)
```

# Questions

## Confidence Interval{.smaller} 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat{p}_1 &= \frac{42}{50}=0.84 \\
\hat{p}_2 &= \frac{34}{50}=0.68 \\[4pt]
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 &= 0.16 \\[6pt]
SE &= \sqrt{
\frac{0.84(1-0.84)}{50}
+
\frac{0.68(1-0.68)}{50}
} \\[6pt]
&= 0.0864 \\[6pt]
95\%\ CI &= 0.16 \pm 1.96(0.0864) \\[4pt]
&= 0.16 \pm 0.1693 \\[4pt]
&=\boxed{(-0.0093,\ 0.3293)}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Interpretation

How do we interpret this?

Why do we not say probability?

# Do my tests agree?

## Not really 

But here is why?

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Observed proportions
p1 <- 42/50
p2 <- 34/50
diff <- p1 - p2

# Null (pooled) SE
p_pool <- (42 + 34)/(50 + 50)

SE_null <- sqrt(
  p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1/50 + 1/50)
)

# CI SE
SE_CI <- sqrt(
  p1*(1-p1)/50 +
  p2*(1-p2)/50
)

# 95% CI
z_star <- 1.96
lower <- diff - z_star*SE_CI
upper <- diff + z_star*SE_CI

# Create x values
x <- seq(-0.15, 0.40, length.out = 1000)

# Data for both panels
df <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    x = x,
    y = dnorm(x, 0, SE_null),
    Panel = "Hypothesis Test: Null Distribution"
  ),
  data.frame(
    x = x,
    y = dnorm(x, diff, SE_CI),
    Panel = "95% Confidence Interval"
  )
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "black") +
  
  # Shade p-value in null distribution
  geom_area(
    data = subset(
      df,
      Panel == "Hypothesis Test: Null Distribution" &
        x >= diff
    ),
    fill = "red",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  
  # Shade the 95% CI in the CI distribution
  geom_area(
    data = subset(
      df,
      Panel == "95% Confidence Interval" &
        x >= lower & x <= upper
    ),
    fill = "skyblue",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Null value = 0
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    color = "darkgreen",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Observed difference
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = diff,
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # CI endpoints
  geom_vline(
    data = data.frame(
      x = c(lower, upper),
      Panel = "95% Confidence Interval"
    ),
    aes(xintercept = x),
    color = "blue",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  facet_wrap(~Panel, ncol = 1) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Why p < 0.05 but the 95% CI Contains 0",
    x = "Difference in Proportions",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal()
```
